newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS - Waigel sees closer NE Europe cooperation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Waigel sees closer NE Europe cooperation.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Monday he was seeking to enhance cooperation among states bordering the Baltic Sea and to attract European Union funds for the region.

Waigel and eight of his North European counterparts began a two-day meeting in Norway's old Hanseatic city of Bergen to discuss economic cooperation around the Baltic Sea and preparations for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Impressed by economic growth rates in Nordic countries and the pace of reform in Poland and the three Baltic States, Germany hopes a modern-day "Hanseatic League" in the region could eventually rival the Mediterranean as an economic force. The Hanseatic League was a chain of cities that dominated trade in Europe's northern seas in medieval times.
"In the European Union a debate is going on how the means shall be distributed among central Europe, the Mediterranean and the possible new members of the European Union," Waigel told reporters.
"It is about a lot of money now in Europe and the question is how to distribute the money," he said during a walk along the harbour of scenic Bergen.
"The question then is what goes to central and eastern Europe... The Mediterranean region is important but it is not European countries," he said.

The informal meeting drew delegations from 10 countries, only four of which are members of the European Union. It follows a similar conference held a year ago in Boltenhagen, a German resort on the Baltic Sea, at the initiative of Waigel.

"Above all this provides the Baltic states with a supplementary relation to the other states and members of the European Union. For the moment they are not all members of the European Union," Waigel told a news conference.

Waigel was holding talks with his Nordic counterparts from Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Iceland as well as Poland and the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinistoe stayed at home with a flu.
The meeting was being hosted by Norway, whose oil-driven economy is the envy of most of Europe.

The world's second largest oil exporter, Norway is projected to run up a budget surplus of 55.4 billion crowns ($8.2 billion) this year and could easily fulfil the Maastricht economic criteria which Germany and other EU member states are now trying to meet for EMU.
Ironically, Norwegians in a referendum in 1994 voted against joining the EU. Iceland also has no plans to join.
But Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland all want membership.
Denmark, an old EU member, has opted out of the EMU, due to start in 1999, following a 1993 referendum.

Sweden and Finland, both of which joined the EU in January 1995, have different approaches with the Swedes undecided on whether to join EMU and the Finns officially in favour of a single currency. ($ = 6.760 Norwegian Crowns)
